easy.heading: Waking Up My Brain With Today's First Puzzle
easy.body:
I started today's easy grid by looking for the most obvious spots. The sum region at 2,0 is a great place to begin because it has to be a 4 to meet the target. I saw that 2,0 was paired with 2,1 to form a domino, so that gave me my first piece. Then I noticed the empty cell at 1,4. Since empty cells act like a zero, I knew that whatever domino I put there would have a zero on that side. I paired 1,4 with 0,4, which meant 0,4 had to be a 4 because of the dominoes I had left.

That 4 at 0,4 was the key for the next section. There is a sum region covering 0,3 and 0,4 that needs to equal 9. Since I already had a 4 at 0,4, the cell at 0,3 had to be a 5. I paired 0,3 with 0,2 to make the [5,4] domino. From there, the rest of the board just fell into place. The greater than constraint at 0,1 needed something bigger than 5, so the 6 from the [4,6] domino fit perfectly when paired with 1,1. It is always so satisfying when the last few pieces just click together like that.

medium.heading: Finding My Groove In The Middle Ground
medium.body:
The medium puzzle today had a few more empty spots and equals constraints that made me stop and think for a second. I zeroed in on the empty cells at 2,5 and 3,0 first. These are essentially freebies if you can figure out which dominoes they belong to. I paired 3,0 with 3,1 and 2,5 with 3,5. This helped me look at the sum region at 3,4 and 3,5 which needs to total 2. Since 3,5 was part of a domino where the other side was empty, I could see that 3,5 was a 2, making 3,4 a 0.

The trickiest part was the equals regions at the top. Cells 0,2 and 1,2 have to be the same, and cells 0,3 and 1,3 also have to be the same. By looking at the dominoes I had left like [6,2] and [6,1], I realized that 1,3 and 2,3 being equal meant they both had to be 6. Once I placed the [6,1] domino across 1,3 and 2,3, the 10 sum at 2,3 and 2,4 was half solved. It took a bit of counting, but eventually, the grid was full and all the totals matched up perfectly.

hard.heading: The Sunday Night Showdown Was A Real Brain Burner
hard.body:
Wow, this hard puzzle really lived up to its name today! I spent a good five minutes just staring at the unequal region on the right side involving cells like 1,7, 2,7, and 3,7. These are tough because you just have to make sure no two numbers are the same. I decided to leave that for last and focus on the sum of 0 at 4,3. That is a huge hint because it means 4,3 must be a 0. I paired it with 3,3 to use the [4,0] domino. This also helped with the sum region of 9 at 3,3 and 3,4, telling me 3,4 had to be a 5.

Another big breakthrough came from the equals regions at the top left. Cells 1,1, 1,2, and 2,2 all have to be the same value. After checking my remaining dominoes, I realized they all had to be 2. This let me place the [3,2] domino at 3,2 and 2,2, which then helped me satisfy the sum of 10 at 3,1 and 3,2. The most stressful part was the very end, making sure that long unequal chain didn't have any repeats. I had to swap the [5,6] and [4,6] dominoes twice before I got the logic right, but I finally saw the light when the last sum of 10 at 4,2 and 5,2 worked out.

explanation.tips: Always look for the empty regions or zero sums first because they narrow down your domino choices immediately. If you get stuck, look for the equals regions that span three or more cells, as these usually only have one or two possible values based on the dominoes you have left in your tray. Don't be afraid to work from the edges inward, especially when there are long chains of unequal constraints.
explanation.learned:
Today I learned that the unequal constraint is much easier to handle if you save it for the very end of the puzzle. It acts as a great way to verify your remaining pieces rather than trying to guess them at the start. I also noticed a recurring pattern where a sum of 10 is often made of a 4 and a 6 when those high-value dominoes are available in the tray.

I also found that checking the orientation of dominoes near the corners can save a lot of time. If a corner cell has a specific sum requirement, it almost always dictates how the two adjacent dominoes must sit. It is like a little logic shortcut that helps prevent having to erase work later on.

faqs.question: What does an empty region mean in the NYT Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: An empty region or a cell marked as empty means that the value of that specific cell is zero. This is very helpful for solving sum constraints or greater than/less than puzzles.

faqs.question: How do you solve the unequal constraint in Pips?
faqs.answer: The unequal constraint means that every cell within that highlighted region must contain a different number. No two cells in that group can have the same value, which is common in harder difficulty puzzles.

faqs.question: Can I reuse dominoes in the same Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: No, you can only use each domino provided in the tray exactly once. A large part of the strategy is keeping track of which dominoes you have already placed on the board.

faqs.question: What is the best strategy for the hard NYT Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: Start with the smallest sum targets like 0 or 1, and the largest ones like 10 or 12. These have the fewest possible combinations, which gives you a solid foundation to solve the more flexible parts of the grid.

faqs.question: Who creates the NYT Pips puzzles?
faqs.answer: The puzzles are usually constructed by experts like Ian Livengood and Rodolfo Kurchan, who are well-known in the puzzle community for their clever logic layouts.
